title: Clean and Unclean Animals
summary: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron which animals Israel may eat. Land animals must have a fully split hoof and chew the cud, water creatures must have fins and scales, a list of birds (mostly birds of prey and scavengers) is forbidden, and among winged insects only locusts, crickets, katydids, and grasshoppers are allowed. The chapter also explains how touching carcasses makes people and objects unclean, and it grounds everything in God's call: be holy, because I am holy.
story: Chapter 10 ended with the priests charged to “distinguish between the holy and the common, between the clean and the unclean” and to teach Israel (10:10-11). Chapters 11 to 15 supply the content of that teaching, working through the areas of daily life where cleanness was at stake: food (11), childbirth (12), skin disease and mold (13-14), and bodily discharges (15). Food comes first because it is the most constant part of life. The Bible's story of food has its own shape. In Genesis God gives plants for food (Genesis 1:29), after the flood he gives Noah every living thing (Genesis 9:3), and now at Sinai Israel's menu is narrowed as a sign of its calling. The food laws became one of the clearest marks of Jewish identity, and later one of the hardest questions the early church had to settle when Gentiles began to join it.
historical:
Deuteronomy 14:3-21 gives a parallel list, close to this one but shorter, which shows how central these rules were to Israel's law. Their effect on Israel's history was large. Archaeologists have noticed that pig bones are rare at the Iron Age hill-country villages usually associated with early Israel, and more common at Philistine cities on the coast, though they debate whether the pattern reflects diet, ecology, or a conscious marker of identity. In the book of Daniel, set among the exiles in Babylon, keeping food laws is already a matter of faithfulness under pressure: Daniel resolves not to defile himself with the king's food (Daniel 1:8).

The sharpest test came around 167 BC, when the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes tried to suppress Jewish practice in Judea. The books of Maccabees, preserved in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and read by Protestants as history rather than Scripture, describe Jews being forced to eat pork and dying rather than do so, among them an aged scribe named Eleazar and a mother with her seven sons. For Jews of the Second Temple period, the rules of Leviticus 11 were not trivia but the line where loyalty to God was tested.
cultural:
Many of the animals are hard to identify, and translations differ. The rock badger of verse 5 is the hyrax, a small, furry animal of rocky hillsides, and the rabbit of verse 6 is most likely the hare. Neither is a true ruminant that brings up its food to chew it again, but both move their jaws constantly as though chewing, and hares re-eat some of their own droppings to digest their food a second time. The chapter classifies animals by what an observer could see, not by modern biology. The same is true of the birds, whose Hebrew names are often uncertain; most on the list seem to be birds of prey or carrion eaters. The bat appears among them because the Hebrew word covers any flying creature.

Impurity from carcasses was not sin, and it did not last long. Touching a dead unclean animal made a person unclean until evening, and washing clothes ended it (verses 24-28). The rules about pots and seed show how people thought impurity moved. A clay pot absorbs what touches it and had to be broken, while wood, cloth, and leather could be washed (verses 32-33). Water spread impurity, so dry seed stayed clean but wet seed did not (verses 37-38). Later Jewish law built an entire body of rules on that verse about moisture and susceptibility. Springs and cisterns stayed clean even when a carcass fell in (verse 36), a merciful exception in a land where water was scarce.
literary: The chapter sorts animals by the same three realms that Genesis 1 fills on the fifth and sixth days, though in a different order: creatures of the land (verses 2-8), of the waters (9-12), and of the air, first birds (13-19) and then winged insects (20-23). It then turns to contact with carcasses (24-40) and to creatures that swarm along the ground (41-43), before ending with the theological reason (44-45) and a summary (46-47). The phrase translated any kind of echoes the Genesis refrain about creatures made according to their kinds. The vocabulary moves between unclean and detestable, stronger words for things Israel must reject entirely. The climax comes in verses 44-45, where the language suddenly rises: “be holy, because I am holy.” This is the first time Leviticus uses the formula, and it will become the motto of chapters 17 to 26. Verse 45 connects the command to the exodus, so the diet of Israel is presented as part of the life of a people God rescued from Egypt.

outline.t: Land animals: split hooves and chewing the cud
Winged insects: only locusts and their kin
Swarming creatures and the call to be holy

doctrines.note: Holiness here reaches the kitchen table. Israel's holiness was meant to show in the most ordinary acts, and the reason given is God's own character: “be holy, because I am holy” (verse 45). Holiness is being set apart for God in everything, not only at the sanctuary.

The chapter uses the realms of creation from Genesis 1 (land, water, and sky) and treats the animal world as God's ordered world. Unclean animals are not evil or cursed; they are God's creatures, simply not for Israel's table. The distinctions reflect God's ordering, not a flaw in what he made.

The food laws marked Israel off from the nations. Leviticus 20:24-26 makes the link explicit: God has set Israel apart from the peoples, so Israel must set apart clean and unclean animals. What Israel ate was a daily reminder of whose people it was.

words.note: Tame, unclean or impure. Uncleanness in Leviticus is a ritual status, not a moral failing or a sin, and much of it is unavoidable in ordinary life. An unclean person could not approach the sanctuary or eat holy food until cleansed. The word appears again and again in chapters 11 to 15.

Sheqets, a detestable thing. It is stronger than unclean and is used here for creatures Israel must avoid entirely, such as water creatures without fins and scales and swarming things. A related word is used elsewhere for idols, which shows how strongly the term expresses rejection.

Qadosh, holy, set apart for God. When used of God it expresses his utter distinctness and moral purity. Verses 44-45 apply it to Israel as a calling: God is holy, so his people must be. First Peter quotes these verses for the church (1 Peter 1:16).

christ: The New Testament addresses this chapter directly. Jesus taught that “Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him,” and Mark adds, “Thus all foods are clean” (Mark 7:18-19). In Acts 10 Peter sees a vision of unclean animals and hears, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15). The vision is about more than food, since it prepares Peter to enter the house of the Gentile Cornelius. That is the key. The food laws marked the line between Israel and the nations, and in Christ, Paul says, God has made the two one, “by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees” (Ephesians 2:15). Colossians calls such regulations “a shadow of the things to come,” while “the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:17). The command to be holy remains. Peter repeats it word for word, “Be holy, because I am holy” (1 Peter 1:16), and applies it to conduct rather than diet.

hard.q: Why were these animals unclean, and do Christians still need to keep these laws?
hard.a:
The chapter gives no reason for particular animals, and interpreters have proposed several. The hygiene view, held in part by the medieval Jewish scholar Maimonides, sees the laws as protecting health, since pork and shellfish can carry disease; critics note that many clean animals carry disease too and that the Bible never gives health as the reason. Another view holds that forbidden animals were associated with pagan worship, which fits a few cases but not most. The anthropologist Mary Douglas, in Purity and Danger (1966), argued that clean animals are those that fit their realm completely, like fish with fins and scales, while unclean ones blur the categories, so the laws taught Israel about wholeness and order. Jacob Milgrom stressed reverence for life, noting that many forbidden creatures are predators or carrion eaters and that the laws, together with the ban on blood, limited the taking of life. The text's own reason is holiness and separation (verses 44-45; 20:24-26), and Deuteronomy 14:21 notes that a foreigner could eat what an Israelite could not, which shows the laws marked Israel's calling rather than a universal diet.

On Christian practice, most churches follow the New Testament passages that declare all foods clean and treat the food laws as fulfilled in Christ. Some Christians, including Seventh-day Adventists, continue to avoid meats the chapter calls unclean, and many Messianic Jewish believers keep the food laws as part of their Jewish identity. Paul's counsel in Romans 14 asks believers on each side not to judge the other.

questions: Israel's holiness reached what it ate every day. Where in ordinary life, rather than only in worship, does your faith show?

The food laws marked Israel off from its neighbors, and the New Testament says Christ broke down that barrier. What new marks of difference should Christians carry, and what barriers do they sometimes build that God has torn down?
Paul told Christians who disagreed about food not to judge one another. What disagreements among believers today call for the same restraint?
